name: Sara Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice lineworker with a rural electric co-op, so our lines run through farmland and a lot of forest. Most days we're replacing old poles, trimming around lines, or fixing whatever a storm or a falling tree did overnight. The co-op's small, twelve of us on the line side, and I'm the newest. I love the outdoors part and I hate the paperwork, which is why I do most of mine with an AI app on my phone now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the AI app fit into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I photograph the job sheet and the app turns my notes into the format the office wants, and I quiz myself on theory at lunch. I also used it to translate an old German manual for a recloser we've got, which made the crew laugh. I'm not great at the job yet, I still fumble the hot sticks, but I'm learning fast. Tomas, my partner, teaches maths at the high school, and between us we've saved a good chunk, about eight months, plus some index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, honestly, because I like the tools. I'd post something like: turns out the real upgrade is still a good crew and a bucket truck. People in the co-op would tease me about it for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes for me. The co-op's members still need power, the trees still fall on lines, and I still have three years left on my apprenticeship. My job was safe before and it's safe now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the apps for paperwork and study, because they still save me half an hour a day. I'd push the co-op to try drone inspections, which they've been talking about for two years. And I'd keep putting money into index funds every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little disappointed, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why drones, if nothing radical changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because walking forty kilometres of line through the forest to look for a cracked insulator is slow and dangerous in winter. A drone does that in a morning. That's not AI hype, it's just a good tool, and I'd want to be the one who flies it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this world, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Storms, honestly. We've had three big ones in two years, and the co-op's budget is tight. If members vote down a rate rise, we'd get fewer new hires, but I'd still have my spot.

say: I'd say it's a **shame**, because I like the tools.
I'd post that the real upgrade is still **a good crew** and a bucket truck.
think: Privately, **nothing changes**: trees fall, members need power, the apprenticeship continues.
Her job was **safe before** and stays safe.
do: Keep using **AI apps** for paperwork and study to save half an hour a day.
Push the co-op to trial **drone inspections** of forest lines.
Keep adding to **index funds** each month.
feel: She feels **calm**, with a touch of disappointment.
S0.quote: Walking forty kilometres of line through the forest to look for a cracked insulator is slow and dangerous in winter.
fieldNote: She's an **early adopter** even when the technology underdelivers.
Her real pressure is **storms** and a tight co-op budget, not AI.
She wants to be the one who **flies the drone**.

steps.text: Keep using the AI app for job sheets and theory quizzes
Propose a drone inspection trial to the co-op manager
Add to her index funds every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version, if we share it fairly. AI does the paperwork, the planning gets better, and lineworkers spend more time on the actual lines. Online I'd argue for the savings going to members' bills and workers' training, not just cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's great for me. I already use these tools, so I'd be the one in our crew who helps the others get the hang of it. Tomas is fine too, teachers aren't on that card. The only people I'd worry about are the two women in the co-op office who do billing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A drone pilot licence costs about eight hundred, and I'd pay for it myself this winter. I'd offer to run a lunch session for the crew on the job-sheet app. And I'd talk to the co-op board about retraining the billing staff instead of letting them go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit excited. It feels like a world I'm built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the billing staff yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to come to the lunch session too, honestly. One of them, Marta, is fifty-eight and terrified of computers, but she knows every member by name. That's worth something, and I'd say so at the board meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it feels like a world you're built for. Is there a part you'd find hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the junior who tells the old guys how to use an app. That's awkward. I'd have to do it without making anybody feel stupid, especially the foreman.

I'd argue savings should go to **members' bills** and workers' training.

steps.text: Pay about eight hundred for a drone pilot licence this winter
Run a lunch session on the job-sheet app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public planning, now, not after. The grid is public infrastructure, and if AI and robots are coming for it, the gains should go to everyone. Online I'd be arguing for a shorter week, retraining money, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's two problems at different times. Tomas is in the first wave, because AI that can do any thinking work can teach maths, at least the lesson-planning and marking side, in 2028. My robots come around 2031, so I'd have three years, and I'd use them to be the person who runs the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full speed on the drone licence and then a robotics course, whatever the co-op will pay for and the rest myself. I'd move a chunk of savings out of index funds into cash, so we've got two years of Tomas's pay covered if he loses hours. And I'd ask the co-op for a role in their tech rollout before they hire someone from outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly for Tomas. For me it's a race I think I can win, but it's still a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd probably say teaching is about the kids, not the marking, and he'd be partly right. But a school board with a tight budget will cut teachers if AI can tutor. We'd talk about him training as a counsellor, maybe, something with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you two be, money-wise, after the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine for a year or two, with my pay and the savings. I'm the main earner already, which is funny for an apprentice. But if he lost his job and mine went in 2031, the index funds wouldn't last long.

say: I'd demand **public planning** now, since the grid is public infrastructure.
I'd argue online for a **shorter week** and retraining money.
think: Privately, her partner's **teaching job** is in the first wave in 2028.

steps.text: Finish the drone licence and enrol in a robotics course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to build a plan, and the co-op is a good place to start because members own it. I'd want them to vote on how robots get used. That's what I'd say at the annual meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be a journeyman with drones and robot experience by 2031. Tomas would have time to move into counselling. And robots at 2034 is far enough off that I'd be leading the co-op's robot crew, not competing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone licence this winter and the robotics course next year, calmly. I'd keep the index funds, because there's time for them to grow. And I'd ask the co-op to send me to a trade show on line-maintenance robots, so I see what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fine way. I'd mostly be curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said members should vote. What would you want them to vote for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots should take the dangerous jobs first, like storm work at night, and nobody on the crew gets laid off, only retired. That's fair, I think, and members would back it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomas do differently with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe buy a house now, while we both have steady pay. In the two-year version I'd never risk it. With five, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get this right for everyone, so let's not waste it. I'd want unions and co-ops pushing for robots to take the worst jobs first. Online I'd say it's an opportunity, if it's shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one I'm most comfortable with. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven with a decade on the lines and the drone and robot skills. I'd probably be running maintenance for the co-op's machines by 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my plan steady: licence, robotics, journeyman, then maybe a two-year technical diploma in power systems. I'd keep investing every month. Tomas and I would buy a house and maybe think about kids around thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I feel ready for this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would AI change that plan at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this one. With ten years, I'd feel I can raise a kid and still keep up. In the fast one I'd wait, because I wouldn't know what world they'd grow into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about this picture that you'd find hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching the older crew members retire early because they don't want to learn. I'd miss them, and I'd feel a bit guilty, being the one who's fine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tomas gets hit first and I'd be racing the robots. What would help is the co-op paying for robot training for its own crews, and public money for teachers to retrain into roles with kids, not marking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the dangerous parts. People talk about robots taking jobs, but nobody asks the person who climbs in an ice storm at three in the morning whether they'd like a robot to do it. Sometimes I would.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the person who climbs in an ice storm at three in the morning whether they'd like a robot to do it.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old apprentice** with a rural electric co-op, working forest lines and storms.
She uses **AI tools every day** for paperwork and study, and wants to fly inspection drones.
Her partner is a **maths teacher**, and they have about eight months saved plus index funds.
She's **calm** in most pictures, seeing herself as the one who runs the robots.
She turns **anxious** in the fast picture because her partner's teaching job goes first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her **partner's job** goes first and she'd be racing robots.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op paying for **robot training**, and public money for teachers to retrain.
